opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think a lot of people in our field have had the order of things backwards for a while. The assumption was that if you build a good enough model, whether it's protein structure prediction, generative design, or something that predicts binding affinity, the impact will just follow. But in practice a model sitting in a GitHub repo, or behind an API that expects perfectly formatted inputs, barely touches the people who could actually use it.

Think about who the end user is. It's often a bench scientist, maybe a medicinal chemist or a protein engineer, who is brilliant at their domain but isn't going to spin up GPUs, wrangle conda environments, or figure out which of fifteen checkpoints is the right one. If using your model takes three days of setup, they won't use it, and the model's quality doesn't matter at that point.

The second piece is that biology is inherently a workflow problem, not a single-inference problem. Nobody runs a structure prediction and stops there. You generate candidates, filter them, score them with a few different models, check developability, look at the structures, compare against what you already know, and then decide what's worth the money to synthesize and test in the lab. The value is in chaining those steps together sensibly, and that orchestration is a product problem as much as a modeling one.

Third, and this is the part I find most exciting, the product layer is where you close the loop with experiments. When a scientist designs something, sends it to the wet lab, and gets results back, that data is incredibly valuable. If your product captures it and feeds it into the next round of design, you get a flywheel where the models improve on the problems people actually care about, rather than on whatever benchmark happened to be available.

And finally there's trust. Biologists are rightly skeptical. They want to know why a model suggested something, how confident it is, and how it compares to alternatives. Good interfaces that surface uncertainty, let people visualize and interrogate results, and fit how they already think about the science are what turn a skeptical user into someone who relies on these tools every day.

So it's not that models don't matter; they obviously do. But a great model with a poor product layer is a research artifact, and a good model with a great product layer actually changes how science gets done.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that a biological model, no matter how good, doesn't do anything by itself. A protein structure prediction or a binder design is a hypothesis. The thing that actually matters is whether a scientist can turn that hypothesis into an experiment, and then whether the result of that experiment makes the next prediction better. The product layer is where that loop either closes or doesn't.

And I think people coming from the language model world underestimate how different the user is. A software engineer will tolerate a rough CLI and a weird API because they live in that world. A wet-lab biologist mostly won't, and honestly shouldn't have to. They're thinking in terms of constructs, plates, assays, cost per experiment, how many weeks until they get a readout. If the model's output doesn't map onto those units, it just doesn't get used, and the best model in the world sitting on a GPU nobody queries is worth zero.

There's also a data argument that I think is the deeper one. Biology is bottlenecked on labeled experimental data far more than on architecture. The labs generating that data are the ones running experiments every day. If your product is actually in their workflow, you're the one who sees what got tested, what worked, what failed, and why. That feedback is the moat, not the weights. Models get commoditized pretty fast. A tight loop between a specific lab's experiments and a model that's learning from them is much harder to replicate.

So the way I'd put it is: the model is the engine, but the product is the whole car, and in biology the road is really bumpy. You can have the best engine and still not get anywhere if you haven't built the rest of the vehicle for the terrain.

astra-6.text:
Because the model is only one part of getting to a useful result. A scientist has a question, an experiment they can run, and constraints on time and resources. The product layer has to connect what the model can do to that actual workflow.

If you generate a biological design, how does someone decide whether to trust it? How do they compare it with alternatives, understand its limitations, and get it into an experiment? And when the experimental results come back, how do those results inform what they try next?

That loop is where a lot of the value comes from. Model quality matters enormously, but so does making the model usable by someone who understands the biology and needs to make a decision. A great product helps them turn a prediction into something they can test and learn from.

sol-6.1.text:
Because a model’s capabilities only matter if someone can use them to make a better decision. In biology, there’s a lot between getting a prediction and knowing what experiment to run next. You have to understand the inputs, interpret the output, and decide how much confidence to place in it.

The product layer connects those pieces. It puts the model into a scientist’s workflow and helps them turn a prediction into something they can test. And then the experimental result can inform the next prediction.

So I think of the model and the product as parts of the same system. A better model expands what’s possible; a better product helps people actually realize that value.
